1.e4 c5 2.Nf3.strategy: Develops the king's knight, controls d4 and e5 and prepares d4 to open the centre. Once d4 is played and the pawns are exchanged, White has an Open Sicilian: a lead in development and kingside space, against Black's central pawn majority and half-open c-file. By far the most common second move, it leads to open, extremely complex play.

1.e4 c5 2.c3.strategy: Prepares d4, so that ...cxd4 can be answered by cxd4 with two pawns in the centre. Black therefore has to counter in the centre at once. If White does get d4 in, an isolated d-pawn and active pieces usually result, in a quieter game than the Open Sicilian.

1.e4 c5 2.Nc3.strategy: Develops a knight and keeps the centre closed for now. White can still reach an Open Sicilian, build up with a kingside fianchetto, or attack on the kingside with the f-pawn. The knight blocks the c-pawn, so the direct fight for d4 is postponed, and Black can develop without trouble.

1.e4 c5 2.b3.name: Sicilian Defence: Snyder Variation
1.e4 c5 2.b3.background: Named after Robert M. Snyder, a US Chess Federation master, who published a book on the system in 1977. Nigel Short has used it occasionally, and it is a favourite of the Georgian grandmaster Tamaz Gelashvili.
1.e4 c5 2.b3.strategy: Prepares Bb2, aiming down the long diagonal at d4, e5 and Black's kingside, and keeps other set-ups open. The move does nothing for the centre at once, so Black can develop freely. Sound, but it gives White less than the main second moves.

1.e4 c5 2.d3.strategy: Prepares a kingside fianchetto, quick development and early castling, and usually leads to a closed game. The structure is solid but makes no claim on d4, so Black builds freely.

1.e4 c5 2.d4.strategy: Opens the centre at once: after 2...cxd4 3.c3 dxc3 4.Nxc3 White gives a pawn for quick development, open c- and d-files and pressure on f7 from a bishop on c4. Theory holds that this is not enough for the pawn, but the many traps make it a hard test for an unprepared opponent. Black can also decline the pawn and reach quieter lines.

1.e4 c5 2.f4.strategy: Controls e5 and prepares to develop the knight and a bishop, aiming for a kingside attack. Played at once, it allows 2...d5 3.exd5 Nf6, when Black regains the pawn on d5 or gets quick development for it, which several authors regard as Black's best answer. White therefore usually develops the queen's knight first, which makes ...d5 harder, and plays f4 a move later.

1.e4 c5 2.g3.name: Sicilian Defence: Lasker–Dunne Attack
1.e4 c5 2.g3.background: The line occurred in the 1866 match between Steinitz and Anderssen, and Mark Taimanov sometimes played it.
1.e4 c5 2.g3.strategy: Prepares a kingside fianchetto and keeps the centre closed, often leading to a slow, manoeuvring game. Black can strike at once with 2...d5, since 3.exd5 Qxd5 hits the rook on h1 through the gap on g2; White blocks the diagonal with a developing move and can then build up in the centre. Sound, but less ambitious than the main lines.

1.e4 c5 2.Na3.name: Sicilian Defence: Kronberger Variation
1.e4 c5 2.Na3.background: An eccentric move brought back into prominence by Vadim Zvjaginsev at the 2005 Russian Chess Championship Superfinal, where he played it three times, drawing twice and beating Alexander Khalifman.
1.e4 c5 2.Na3.strategy: Heads for a more active square and keeps c3 free for the c-pawn, away from the main lines of theory. For now the knight stands on the rim and does nothing for d4, so Black can take the centre freely. It is sound but gives White little.

1.e4 c5 2.Ne2.name: Sicilian Defence: Keres Variation
1.e4 c5 2.Ne2.background: It was a favourite of Paul Keres, whose name it carries, and it shares its ideas with the Chameleon System of 2.Nc3 and 3.Nge2.
1.e4 c5 2.Ne2.strategy: Keeps the choice open between an Open Sicilian and a closed set-up, while the f-pawn stays free to advance. For now the knight blocks the f1-bishop, and the early Ne2 is not very challenging, so Black can develop without trouble.

1.e4 c5 2.a3.name: Sicilian Defence: Mengarini Variation
1.e4 c5 2.a3.strategy: Prepares b4, so that ...cxb4 can be met by axb4 and the c-pawn is deflected from the fight for d4, but it spends a tempo on the rim. After 2...Nc6 the push no longer works, since 3.b4 cxb4 4.axb4 Nxb4 simply wins a pawn, and Black develops freely.

1.e4 c5 2.a4.name: Sicilian Defence: Myers Attack, with a4
1.e4 c5 2.a4.strategy: Stops ...b5 but spends a tempo on the rim and weakens b4 for good, since the a-pawn can no longer guard it, and a black knight from c6 can use the square. Black develops freely.

1.e4 c5 2.b4.strategy: Offers the b-pawn to deflect the c-pawn and then take the centre with d4. After 2...cxb4 3.a3 d5, now considered Black's best, White has too little for the pawn and must even avoid 4.exd5 Qxd5 5.axb4, which loses the rook on a1 to 5...Qe5+.

1.e4 c5 2.c4.name: Sicilian Defence: Staunton–Cochrane Variation
1.e4 c5 2.c4.strategy: Resembles an English Opening with the king's pawn already on e4, but leaves d4 without pawn cover, since neither the c- nor the e-pawn can return to guard it. Black answers with ...Nc6 and ...e5 and gets a comfortable game, with d4 as a lasting outpost for a knight.

1.e4 c5 2.f3.strategy: Supports e4 but takes f3 from the king's knight and opens the e1–h4 diagonal to the king. Black develops freely, while White's kingside pieces lack good squares.

1.e4 c5 2.h3.strategy: Takes g4 from Black's pieces but spends a tempo without any gain in the centre or development. Black develops freely, and the pawn on h3 rarely proves useful.

1.e4 c5 2.h4.name: Sicilian Defence: Myers Attack, with h4
1.e4 c5 2.h4.strategy: Spends a tempo on the rook's pawn and weakens g4 for good, since the h-pawn can no longer guard it, with nothing gained for the centre or development. Black develops freely, and the advanced pawn makes castling short less safe for White.

1.e4 c5 2.Qe2.strategy: Supports e4 but blocks the f1-bishop and brings the queen out before the minor pieces. Black develops freely, and White has nothing in the centre to show for the tempo.

1.e4 c5 2.Qf3.strategy: Takes f3 from the king's knight and exposes the queen, which ...Nc6 and ...Nd4 attack with gain of time, the knight also hitting c2, which the queen no longer guards. Black develops freely while White has to move the queen again.

1.e4 c5 2.Qg4.name: Sicilian Defence: Amazon Attack
1.e4 c5 2.Qg4.strategy: Eyes g7 and d7, but both are defended, so nothing is threatened. 2...Nf6 hits the queen and the e4-pawn at once, and the queen has to move again while Black develops with gain of time.

1.e4 c5 2.Qh5.strategy: Attacks c5 along the fifth rank and eyes f7, but brings the queen out too early. 2...Nf6 hits it: 3.Qxc5 Nxe4 regains the pawn with gain of time, and 3.Qh4 only displaces the queen, so Black gets a comfortable game.

1.e4 c5 2.Be2.strategy: Prepares Nf3 and quick castling, but the bishop is passive on e2 and no longer guards g2: after 2...d5 3.exd5 Qxd5 the queen hits g2, and White must spend a move blocking the diagonal.

1.e4 c5 2.Bd3.strategy: Blocks the d-pawn, and with it the c1-bishop, until the bishop on d3 moves again. Black develops freely, while White needs another bishop move to free the queenside.

1.e4 c5 2.Bc4.name: Sicilian Defence: Bowdler Attack
1.e4 c5 2.Bc4.background: Though once played at the highest level, for example in Anderssen–Wyvill, London 1851, it is popular today only among club players and beginners who are unfamiliar with the Sicilian.
1.e4 c5 2.Bc4.strategy: Aims at f7 and prepares quick castling, but the bishop is exposed: after 2...e6 Black follows with ...d5, opening the centre with gain of time on the bishop. The attack on f7 is easy to meet, and Black gets a comfortable game.

1.e4 c5 2.Bb5.strategy: Develops the bishop without a target, and ...a6 drives it back with loss of time; 3.Ba4 even loses it to 3...b5 4.Bb3 c4, which traps the bishop. Black gains queenside space with ...b5 as well and develops comfortably.

1.e4 c5 2.Nh3.name: Sicilian Defence: Brick Variation
1.e4 c5 2.Nh3.strategy: Heads for f4 or g5 but sits on the rim, where it neither contests d4 nor supports e4. After ...d6 the c8-bishop eyes it, and ...Bxh3 gxh3 would wreck White's kingside pawns.

1.e4 c5 2.e5.strategy: Gains space and stops ...Nf6, but the lone pawn adds no pressure on the centre. ...Nc6 and ...d6 attack it, and White has to spend time supporting it.

1.e4 c5 2.g4.name: Sicilian Defence: Grob Variation
1.e4 c5 2.g4.strategy: Loosens the long diagonal and the squares f4 and h4 for no gain. After 2...d5 3.exd5 Qxd5 the queen hits the rook on h1, and after 4.Nf3 Bxg4 Black has won the g-pawn and pins the knight against the queen.

1.e4 c5 2.Ke2.name: Sicilian Defence: King David's Opening
1.e4 c5 2.Ke2.strategy: Gives up castling and blocks the f1-bishop and the queen's diagonal to h5. Black develops and opens the centre against a king that has nowhere safe to go.

1.e4 c5 2.Ba6.strategy: Hangs the bishop: 2...bxa6 or 2...Nxa6 wins it for nothing, because nothing defends a6.

1.e4 c5.name: Sicilian Defence
1.e4 c5.background: Giulio Cesare Polerio analysed it in a manuscript of 1594. In 1813 Jacob Henry Sarratt standardised the English name, after an old Italian manuscript that spoke of “il gioco siciliano”, the Sicilian game. Revived by Botvinnik, Boleslavsky, Bronstein and Najdorf in the 1940s and 1950s, it became, in the words of Modern Chess Openings (1990), the most played and most analysed opening at both club and master level.

1.e4 c5 2.b3 b6.name: Sicilian Defence: Czerniak Attack, Queen Fianchetto Variation
1.e4 c5 2.b3 b6.strategy: Mirrors White's plan: the bishop on b7 will pressure the e4 pawn, which has no defender yet, and fight for the long diagonal. Both queen's bishops aim at the opposing kingside, and the game becomes a manoeuvring duel.

1.e4 c5 2.b3 d5.strategy: Strikes at e4 at once, before White's pieces are out, and claims the centre with a pawn the queen can recapture. It is a sharp way to meet 2.b3, since White cannot calmly fianchetto with the e4 pawn under pressure.

1.e4 c5 2.b3 Nc6.strategy: The main reply: Black develops a piece, eyes the d4 and b4 squares and keeps every set-up open. White's b-pawn move is slow, so Black can build a normal Sicilian structure and wait for White to show what the fianchetto achieves.

1.e4 c5 2.b3 e6.strategy: Solid: Black opens the king's bishop and prepares ...d5 to claim the centre, accepting a slightly slower development. The pawn on c5 keeps White from building a broad centre, and Black gets an easy, comfortable game.

1.e4 c5 2.b3 d5 3.Bb2.name: Sicilian Defence: Euwe Attack, Prins Gambit
1.e4 c5 2.b3 d5 3.Bb2.strategy: Ignores the tension and develops, offering e4 for rapid development and an open long diagonal pointing at g7. White has to show that this is enough for the pawn, since the simple exchange on d5 is the more solid way to proceed.

1.e4 c5 2.b3 d5 3.exd5.strategy: Settles the tension on White's terms: after the queen recaptures, Nc3 attacks it with a gain of time, and the bishop on b2 later pressures the long diagonal. Black gets an open centre and White a lead in development, which the b3 set-up is built for.

1.e4 c5 2.b3 d5 3.Nc3.strategy: Develops and adds a defender to e4, but invites ...d4, which gains space and drives the knight back. It also blunts the long diagonal for the bishop White intends to put on b2, so White's pieces become awkward.

1.e4 c5 2.c4 Nc6.strategy: Develops with a stake in d4: the c-pawn can no longer support a d4 advance, so the knight and later pawn moves fight for the centre. Black stays flexible, and the knight has a good square without weakening anything.

1.e4 c5 2.c4 d6.strategy: A solid reply: it guards e5, opens the c8-bishop and keeps all the knights' options open. The cost is a slightly passive game, since White has more space in the centre and Black has to play carefully to free the position.

1.e4 c5 2.c4 g6.strategy: Prepares to fianchetto the king's bishop, which will press on the long diagonal and the centre. Black commits neither the d- nor the e-pawn, but White gets time to clamp down on the centre with the c4 and e4 pawns, so Black has to find counterplay.

1.e4 c5 2.c4 e6.strategy: A solid reply that aims for ...d5, the freeing move 2.c4 is meant to prevent, and opens the f8-bishop. The cost is that the c8-bishop stays shut in for now and Black develops a little slowly.

1.e4 c5 2.c4 d6 3.Nc3.strategy: The natural developing move: the knight controls d5, supports the e4 pawn and adds to the grip of the pawns on c4 and e4 on the centre. White plays for a slow positional game with more space.

1.e4 c5 2.c4 d6 3.Nf3.strategy: Develops towards the centre and prepares d4. The e4 pawn is loose for the moment, so ...Nf6 has to be answered at once, most simply by Nc3, but White keeps the option of a central break with the c4 and e4 pawns already in place.

1.e4 c5 2.c4 d6 3.g3.strategy: Prepares a kingside fianchetto, so the bishop on g2 will guard e4 and press on the long diagonal. White forgoes a quick d4 for a compact, slow manoeuvring game, which gives Black time to develop freely.

1.e4 c5 2.c4 d6 3.Nc3 Nc6.strategy: Develops a piece against the centre and keeps an eye on d4 and e5 without weakening anything. Black accepts a solid but slightly cramped position and waits for White to commit before choosing a set-up.

1.e4 c5 2.c4 d6 3.Nc3 Nf6.strategy: Develops with an attack on e4, which the knight on c3 guards, so nothing is won but White must keep the pawn supported. Black keeps a flexible structure and a choice between a fianchetto and a central set-up.

1.e4 c5 2.c4 d6 3.Nc3 g6.strategy: Aims the king's bishop at the long diagonal and the knight on c3 in a flexible, solid set-up. The cost is that White's pawns on c4 and e4 can clamp down on d5 and b5, so Black needs to prepare counterplay.

1.e4 c5 2.c4 d6 3.Nc3 Nc6 4.g3.strategy: Prepares the kingside fianchetto, so that the bishop covers the long diagonal and the king gets a safe home. White prefers a compact structure and a long manoeuvring game to a sharp fight in the centre.

1.e4 c5 2.c4 d6 3.Nc3 Nc6 4.Nf3.strategy: Develops towards the centre and prepares d4. If Black takes on d4, White recaptures with the knight and holds a bind on the centre with the pawns on c4 and e4, which Black must undermine. The move commits White to a fight for the centre rather than a fianchetto.

1.e4 c5 2.c4 d6 3.Nc3 Nc6 4.Nge2.strategy: Keeps both a fianchetto and a later d4 available, but the knight on e2 blocks the f1-bishop and has less influence on the centre than on f3. A flexible, non-committal set-up that gives Black time to choose a plan.

1.e4 c5 2.c4 d6 3.Nc3 Nc6 4.g3 h5.name: Sicilian Defence: Gloria Variation
1.e4 c5 2.c4 d6 3.Nc3 Nc6 4.g3 h5.strategy: An aggressive rim-pawn move aimed at ...h4, which would attack the g3 pawn and spoil White's kingside set-up. It costs a tempo and loosens Black's own kingside, so it is playable and surprising rather than a way to gain anything.

1.e4 c5 2.c4 d6 3.Nc3 Nc6 4.g3 g6.strategy: Prepares a fianchetto of Black's own, so the bishop on g7 presses on the long diagonal and the centre. It is the natural, flexible development: the king finds a safe home and Black prepares for a long manoeuvring game with chances for both sides.

1.e4 c5 2.c4 d6 3.Nc3 Nc6 4.g3 e5.strategy: Takes d4 away from White and rules out the central break. The price is a hole on d5, which no black pawn can ever challenge, so White's knight can settle there, and Black accepts a closed game.

1.e4 c5 2.c4 d6 3.Nc3 Nc6 4.g3 Nf6.strategy: Develops with an attack on e4, which the c3 knight guards, so White has to keep the pawn supported while Black keeps the choice between a fianchetto and a central set-up.

1.e4 c5 2.c4 Nc6 3.Nc3.strategy: The natural developing move: the knight controls d5 and supports e4. White builds a hold on the centre and keeps the choice between a slow positional game and a more central plan open.

1.e4 c5 2.c4 Nc6 3.Nf3.strategy: Develops the kingside knight and watches d4 and e5, so White keeps its options open. It commits to nothing yet, but lets Black claim space with an early ...e5, after which the d4 break is hard to achieve.

1.e4 c5 2.c4 Nc6 3.g3.strategy: Chooses the fianchetto before the knights are placed: the bishop on g2 will guard e4 from a safe corner. The price is flexibility, since the queen's knight has not yet chosen its square and Black can settle the centre first.

1.e4 c5 2.c4 Nc6 3.Nc3 g6.strategy: Prepares the king's bishop on the long diagonal, from where it presses on the centre and the queenside. Black does not fight for e5 at once and accepts less space for a compact, sound position with a safe king.

1.e4 c5 2.c4 Nc6 3.Nc3 e5.strategy: Keeps d4 under firm control: the pawn, the c-pawn and the knight all watch it, so White can hardly prepare the central break. Black gives up control of d5, where a white knight can settle, but gets a solid centre and a sound game.

1.e4 c5 2.c4 Nc6 3.Nc3 d6.strategy: A solid, flexible move that opens the c8-bishop and supports a later ...e5. It does not stop White from preparing d4, so Black ends up with less space and less control of the centre than after the immediate pawn move to e5.

1.e4 c5 2.c4 Nc6 3.Nc3 g6 4.g3.strategy: Prepares the bishop on g2 and a safe king. White does not hurry in the centre: the plan is a lasting space advantage and a slow manoeuvring game rather than quick tactics.

1.e4 c5 2.c4 Nc6 3.Nc3 g6 4.Nf3.strategy: Develops the kingside knight without committing the other pieces, so White can still choose between the fianchetto and a quicker central plan. The pawns on c4 and e4 already clamp down on d5; the cost is that White has not yet decided how to meet ...Bg7.

1.e4 c5 2.c4 Nc6 3.Nc3 g6 4.Nge2.strategy: Keeps the choice between a closed set-up and a central break: the knight supports d4 and leaves the f-pawn free to advance. It is a less active square than f3 and blocks the king's bishop's route to e2, so White gains flexibility but no plan.

1.e4 c5 2.c4 Nc6 3.Nc3 g6 4.g3 Bg7.strategy: Completes Black's fianchetto: the bishop on the long diagonal presses on d4 and on the knight on c3 and clears the way for castling. Both sides now have the same compact set-up and play for small positional gains.

1.e4 c5 2.c4 Nc6 3.Nc3 g6 4.g3 Nf6.strategy: Develops the knight with an attack on e4, which the knight on c3 holds for now. Black prepares quick castling and keeps the long diagonal open for the bishop, a natural and flexible set-up that asks White how to place the pieces.

1.e4 c5 2.c4 Nc6 3.Nc3 g6 4.g3 e5.strategy: Occupies the centre with a pawn and covers d4 and f4. It shuts in the bishop that is about to land on g7 and leaves a hole on d5, so Black plays for a solid, closed game and has to keep an eye on that square.

1.e4 c5 2.c4 Nc6 3.Nc3 g6 4.g3 Bg7 5.Bg2.name: English Opening: Symmetrical Variation, Botvinnik System
1.e4 c5 2.c4 Nc6 3.Nc3 g6 4.g3 Bg7 5.Bg2.strategy: Completes White's fianchetto: the bishop protects the e4 pawn and the king is a knight move from castling. Its long diagonal is blocked by its own pawn for now, so White plays for a slow build-up on space and solidity.

1.e4 c5 2.c4 Nc6 3.Nc3 g6 4.g3 Bg7 5.Nf3.strategy: Develops the second knight and watches d4 and e5 before the bishop arrives on g2. White keeps the grip on d5 and builds slowly: an immediate d4 does not work with Black's bishop on g7, since after ...cxd4 Nxd4 Nxd4 the queen's recapture loses to ...Bxd4.

1.e4 c5 2.c4 Nc6 3.Nc3 g6 4.g3 Bg7 5.d3.strategy: Holds e4 with a pawn, which frees the c3 knight from guarding it. White plays a slow, closed game: space on the queenside, a safe king after castling and a possible f-pawn advance later, with few chances for Black to hit the centre.

1.e4 c5 2.d3 Nc6.strategy: Develops the knight against the centre and keeps Black's pawn structure flexible. White has chosen a quiet, slow set-up, so Black can take the initiative in the centre and does not need to rush.

1.e4 c5 2.d3 g6.strategy: Prepares the fianchetto: the king's bishop will press along the long diagonal towards White's queenside while the knights stay flexible. Black reaches a compact, safe set-up and meets White's slow plan with a plan of its own.

1.e4 c5 2.d3 e6.strategy: Prepares ...d5 to challenge e4 while White's pieces are still undeveloped. The price is a closed c8-bishop that has to find another route, but Black gets a solid pawn structure and a clear plan against the quiet d3.

1.e4 c5 2.d3 Nc6 3.c3.strategy: Gives the centre a firm base: c3 supports a later d4 and takes the c3 square from the queen's knight. White builds slowly and solidly, keeping options open and avoiding any early theory.

1.e4 c5 2.d3 Nc6 3.Nf3.strategy: Develops the knight to its natural square, guards e5 and leaves e4 firmly held by the d-pawn. White heads for a compact set-up with a fianchetto and quick castling, aiming for slowly growing space rather than an early fight in the centre.

1.e4 c5 2.d3 Nc6 3.g3.strategy: Heads for the fianchetto at once: the bishop on g2 protects e4 and White castles quickly. The knight on g1 stays free to choose between e2 and f3, but the move leaves the centre to Black for the moment.

1.e4 c5 2.d3 Nc6 3.c3 d6.strategy: Builds a solid chain, opens the c8-bishop and prepares to challenge White's centre. Black keeps the position healthy and flexible and avoids a pawn structure that White could attack.

1.e4 c5 2.d3 Nc6 3.c3 Nf6.strategy: Develops with an immediate attack on e4, which d3 holds but which now ties White down. A push to e5 only loses the pawn: nothing defends it, and the knight on c6 takes it. Black gets easy development and the first say in the centre.

1.e4 c5 2.d3 Nc6 3.c3 e5.strategy: Claims the centre and takes d4 away from White, so the planned central break is hard to carry out. Black gets a broad pawn centre and early space; the price is a hole on d5 and a more committed pawn structure.

1.e4 c5 2.d3 Nc6 3.c3 d6 4.f4.name: Sicilian Defence: Big Clamp Formation
1.e4 c5 2.d3 Nc6 3.c3 d6 4.f4.strategy: Takes space on the kingside and the e5 square under control, building a broad pawn front. It leaves holes behind it, notably on e3 and g3, and commits White to a plan on the kingside that is hard to undo.

1.e4 c5 2.d3 Nc6 3.c3 d6 4.Nf3.strategy: Develops the knight to the centre, covers e5 and prepares d4. If Black allows it, White gets the ideal pair of pawns on d4 and e4, so the quiet moves c3 and d3 become the foundation of a real central plan rather than mere waiting.

1.e4 c5 2.d3 Nc6 3.c3 d6 4.g3.strategy: Chooses the fianchetto: the bishop on g2 protects e4 and the king castles quickly. White plays a slow, closed game with a compact pawn chain, and keeps the central break d4 available for later if Black lets it.

1.e4 c5 2.Na3 Nc6.strategy: Develops the knight to its best square against the eccentric rim knight. It controls d4 and e5, so White's usual central pawn break comes with a pawn offered, and Black can otherwise play as in any Sicilian.

1.e4 c5 2.Na3 d6.strategy: Takes the e5 square and opens the c8 bishop, a flexible reply as in any Sicilian. The rim knight does little for the centre, so Black can aim for a normal set-up and let White's piece find a role.

1.e4 c5 2.Na3 e6.strategy: Prepares a compact set-up with the bishop free to develop and ...d5 available to challenge e4. A solid choice that treats the rim knight as a loss of time for White.

1.e4 c5 2.Na3 Nc6 3.d4.strategy: A pawn offer that does not pay: ...cxd4 wins a pawn that White cannot take back, since the knight on a3 does not reach d4 and Qxd4 loses the queen to ...Nxd4. White gets some development but no compensation for the pawn.

1.e4 c5 2.Na3 Nc6 3.Nf3.strategy: Develops the kingside knight and prepares the central break d4, which now has a piece ready to recapture. The knight on a3 stands badly for the moment, but it can reroute to b5 or c4, and the game becomes an ordinary open Sicilian in which White has spent one move on that detour.

1.e4 c5 2.Na3 Nc6 3.c3.strategy: Prepares d4 with a pawn, so that the break comes with a recapture ready and a solid centre behind it, and the knight on a3 can head for c2 to support it. Black can challenge the centre at once with ...d5 and develop easily, so White gets a sound but modest game.

1.e4 c5 2.Na3 Nc6 3.Bb5.strategy: Attacks the c6 knight, which guards d4 and e5, and prepares quick castling. The bishop takes nothing, though, and ...Nd4 hits it with tempo, so White gains little more than a quiet game with the bishop on the move again.

1.e4 c5 2.Na3 Nc6 3.d4 cxd4.strategy: Takes the pawn and removes the one that attacks c5. White cannot recapture with the queen, since ...Nxd4 would win it, so Black keeps the extra pawn for now. The price is time: only one piece is developed, and White can start to chase the pawn with natural moves.

1.e4 c5 2.Na3 Nc6 3.d4 Nxd4.strategy: Wins the pawn with the knight, which keeps the c-pawn but costs time: Nf3 hits the centralised knight at once and it has to move again while White develops. Black stays a pawn up, but ...cxd4 wins the pawn without losing a tempo.

1.e4 c5 2.Na3 Nc6 3.d4 Nf6.strategy: Develops and eyes e4 but passes up the free pawn. 4.d5 attacks the c6 knight, which has no good square, and White gains space and tempo while Black's knights are driven back. Black throws away its early gain and stands clearly worse.

1.e4 c5 2.Na3 Nc6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Bc4.name: Sicilian Defence: Kronberger Variation, Nemeth Gambit
1.e4 c5 2.Na3 Nc6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Bc4.strategy: A gambit that does not pay: the bishop eyes f7 and is backed by the knight on a3, which covers c4, but White has no quick way back to d4 and no real attack. Black can consolidate and keeps the extra pawn.

1.e4 c5 2.Na3 Nc6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nf3.strategy: Attacks d4 a second time and heads for an ordinary open Sicilian if Black lets it. But ...e5 holds the pawn, since the knight cannot take it, and White must then play for development against the extra pawn with the knight on a3 still out of play. A good move, not the most precise.

1.e4 c5 2.Na3 Nc6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nb5.strategy: Attacks d4 a second time and eyes c7 and d6, but ...e5 holds the pawn and ...a6 then chases the knight away. White loses time for nothing, and Black keeps the extra pawn with a strong centre.

1.e4 c5 2.Na3 Nc6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Bd3.strategy: Develops the bishop first, covering e4, and plays for quick development with a knight to e2 and castling instead of rushing to regain d4. Black keeps the extra pawn for now, but White's pieces come out with pressure on the open lines against it.
